clinicalPearls: Nocturnal enuresis is involuntary voiding during sleep in a child old enough to be expected to have night-time bladder control, generally around five years and older.
It is classified as primary when the child has never achieved a sustained period of night-time dryness and secondary when wetting returns after at least six months of dryness.
Monosymptomatic enuresis involves night-time wetting alone, whereas non-monosymptomatic enuresis is accompanied by daytime lower urinary tract symptoms such as urgency, frequency, or daytime wetting.
Common contributing factors include a family history, delayed maturation of arousal and bladder control, reduced overnight bladder capacity, and relative overnight excess of urine production.
Most primary monosymptomatic enuresis is not caused by serious disease, and evaluation is mainly history, examination, and urinalysis to exclude infection and glycosuria.
Secondary enuresis or associated daytime symptoms warrant closer evaluation for causes such as urinary tract infection, constipation, diabetes, or psychosocial stress.
First-line management emphasises reassurance, education, and behavioural measures, with the enuresis alarm being the most effective long-term intervention for motivated families.
Constipation frequently coexists and, when treated, wetting often improves, so bowel habits should always be assessed.
reference.pathophysiology: Night-time continence depends on the balance between overnight urine production, bladder storage capacity, and the ability to either suppress bladder contractions during sleep or wake in response to a full bladder. Enuresis arises when this balance fails: some children produce a relatively large volume of urine at night, some have a smaller functional bladder capacity or overactive bladder, and many have a high arousal threshold so a full or contracting bladder does not wake them. These factors, strongly influenced by genetic predisposition and developmental maturation, often coexist. Constipation can reduce functional bladder capacity and provoke bladder overactivity, and secondary enuresis may reflect an acquired medical or psychosocial trigger.
additionalDifferentials: Overactive bladder or other daytime voiding dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis to screen for infection and glucosuria
Assessment of bowel habits for constipation
Bladder diary of daytime symptoms and voiding pattern
Blood glucose if polyuria or other features suggest diabetes
Renal or bladder imaging only when structural or neurological pathology is suspected
redFlags: New-onset (secondary) enuresis with weight loss, polyuria, or polydipsia
Daytime incontinence, straining, or a poor urinary stream
Significant behavioural change or evidence of psychosocial distress or abuse
reference.prognosis: Primary monosymptomatic enuresis has a high rate of spontaneous resolution with age, and treatment can accelerate dryness; the outlook is generally excellent, though relapses can occur and cases with daytime symptoms may need more prolonged management.
pitfalls: Treating the child punitively or blaming the child for an involuntary problem
Overlooking coexisting constipation as a contributor
Failing to distinguish monosymptomatic from non-monosymptomatic enuresis before choosing therapy
Missing an underlying cause of secondary enuresis such as infection or diabetes
